Multi-purpOse displacement Behavior Identifier Digital Image Correlation Tool

Sub-pixel displacement tracking across DEMs, satellite imagery, and fixed cameras. Developed at SLF Davos by the Alpine Remote Sensing Group.

Get Started Request Access

docs.title: What MOBI-DIC can do
docs.text:
• Native QGIS plugin — ready in minutes

    Install once and run directly inside QGIS. The tabbed dialog guides you through every step — configuring single-pair or multi-date time series inputs, tuning DIC parameters, filtering vectors, and loading results with automatic symbology. Run configurations can be saved, reloaded, and shared. Displacement outputs land directly in the QGIS layer tree for immediate further analysis.

  • 3D surface displacement from DEMs

    Computes East-West, North-South, and vertical displacement from repeat DEMs. Correlation runs on hillshade or orientation images; the secondary DEM is then shifted back by the measured horizontal offsets before computing vertical change, so the elevation component is free of horizontal motion bias.

    Output: 3D displacement and velocity as GeoTIFFs (East-West, North-South, vertical); raw sparse results as HDF5, with optional GeoPackage export of sparse points.

  • 2D displacement from optical imagery

    Measures surface motion from any georeferenced image pair (orthophotos, satellite scenes, or UAV mosaics) with sub-pixel accuracy. Automatic co-registration removes sensor offsets before correlation.

    Output: 2D displacement and velocity as GeoTIFFs (East-West, North-South); raw sparse results as HDF5, with optional GeoPackage export of sparse points.

  • Pixel displacement from non-georeferenced imagery

    Measures pixel-level motion from non-georeferenced image pairs: fixed cameras, time-lapse sequences, or scanner imagery. Optional AI segmentation masks static background regions (sky, water) before correlation.

    Output: Pixel-unit displacement images; raw sparse results as HDF5, with optional GeoPackage export of sparse points.

  • Post-processing & outlier filtering

    Two independent filters — neighbourhood coherence and iterative neighbour similarity — remove outliers without re-running DIC. Thresholds can be tuned interactively and filtered results exported as GeoPackage or PNG.

  • Google Earth export & 3D visualisation

    Export displacement rasters and vector arrow fields as KMZ directly from the plugin. Results open in Google Earth Pro for interactive 3D inspection, with optional TimeSpan tags for animated time-series playback.

  • Print layout builder

    Create publication-ready displacement maps with one click. Choose from dedicated displacement colormaps, overlay hillshade or satellite basemaps, and open the result directly in QGIS's print layout editor for PDF or PNG export.

  • CLI & headless batch processing

    Drive the full pipeline from YAML config files — on a desktop, a server, or inside an automated workflow. Sweep multiple resolutions and window sizes in a single run, with all outputs written automatically. No GUI required.

docs.title: Security
docs.text: This page explains what MOBI-DIC installs on your machine, where the packages come from, and how their integrity is verified.

docs.title: What gets installed
docs.text:
When you click Install DIC Environment in the plugin settings, pixi downloads a set of Python packages from conda-forge — a community-maintained, openly reviewed package repository.

The packages installed depend on the build variant you received:

Base build (DEM + Optical)Full build (+ Webcam / AI) Package Purpose python 3.12 Runtime numpy, scipy Numerical computing pandas Tabular data handling geopandas, shapely, pyproj Geospatial vector data rasterio, gdal, affine GeoTIFF / raster I/O scikit-image, pillow Image processing h5py HDF5 output files pyyaml YAML config parsing requests Background map tile fetching matplotlib, matplotlib-scalebar Plotting and visualisation tqdm, joblib, psutil Progress, parallelism, system info

All packages from the Base build, plus:

Package Purpose pytorch, torchvision Deep learning runtime transformers HuggingFace SegFormer model (AI segmentation)

No other software, services, or browser extensions are installed. The environment lives entirely in ~/.slf-dic/ (macOS/Linux) or %USERPROFILE%\.slf-dic\ (Windows) and does not modify your system Python or QGIS Python installation.

docs.title: Package integrity
docs.text:
Every package is pinned to an exact version and verified by SHA256 hash before installation. This means:

  • You always receive exactly the same packages as tested at release time.
  • A corrupted or tampered download is detected and rejected automatically — pixi will refuse to install a package that does not match its recorded hash.
  • Packages cannot silently drift to a newer (or older) version between installs.

The full pinned package list with hashes is embedded in the plugin ZIP as pixi.lock and is not downloaded from the internet at install time.

docs.title: Network access
docs.text:
The tool makes outbound network requests in two situations:

When What To where First install Download Python packages conda-forge mirrors (HTTPS) During DIC run (optional) Fetch background map tiles OpenStreetMap / user-configured tile server

There is no telemetry, no licence phone-home, and no data upload of any kind. Once the environment is installed, the tool can run fully offline (background maps will not load without internet, but DIC processing is unaffected).

docs.title: Vulnerability scanning
docs.text:
Before each release, all bundled packages are scanned for known CVEs using trivy.

What this means in practice: all findings in past scans have been low-severity Denial-of-Service issues that require an attacker to provide a specially crafted input file. For a scientific tool processing your own data, this does not represent a realistic threat. No remote code execution or data-theft vulnerabilities have been found.

If you have a security concern, contact us at mobi-dic@slf.ch.

docs.title: Configuration Reference
docs.text:
All three pipelines share the same YAML structure: io, batch, and dic_params sections. Pass the config file to any processing script with the --config flag — see CLI & Batch Processing for the full invocation commands.

Where to find your config file:

  • Both builds — starter config files are included in the distribution ZIP (config_dic4dem.yml, config_dic4optical.yml, config_dic4webcam.yml). Edit them directly before running. In the pipeline-only build they are inside slf-dic-python/; in the QGIS + CLI build they are in sample_configs/.
  • QGIS users — you can also use the 📋 Copy Run Command button in the plugin dialog to generate a config from the current dialog state and copy the matching shell command to the clipboard.

docs.title: Complete examples
docs.text:
These match the starter config files shipped with the distribution. Replace all paths with your own.

DEMOpticalWebcam 
io:
  base_run_tag: "MyProject_DEM"
  dem_primary:  "/path/to/dem_before.tif"
  dem_secondary: "/path/to/dem_after.tif"
  output_dir:   "/path/to/output"

batch:
  base_dem_res: 1.0          # (1)!
  target_resolutions: [1]    # (2)!
  window_sizes: [64]         # (3)!

dic_params:
  rescale_results: true
  export_sparse_gpkg: true
  OR: 1                      # (4)!
  co_f: 1                    # (5)!
  co_os: 2
  coreg_method: "bbox"       # (6)!
  coreg_bbox: [minx, miny, maxx, maxy]
  os: 4                      # (7)!
  skip_factor: 4             # (8)!
  refcode: "EPSG:2056"
  auto_reproject_to_utm: false
  debug_mode: false
  n_workers: 1

  VectorFilter:
    Enabled: false           # (9)!
    OutputTxt: false
    OutputGpkg: true
    OutputPlot: false
    PlotResult: false
    HillshadeTif: "/path/to/dem_before.tif"
    PlotWMS: false
    WMSLayer: "satellite"
    PlotHillshade: false
    PlotBackgroundXYZ: true
    BlackArrows: true
    MaxMagnitude: 10.0
    ColorMax: 10
    BackgroundAlpha: 0.6
    Downsample: 10
    ThrMin: -100
    ThrMax: 100
  1. Native pixel spacing of your input DEMs in metres. Used as the reference for resampling.
  2. Resolution(s) to resample to before running DIC. Use a list like [1, 2] to run multiple passes in one batch.
  3. Correlation window size(s) in pixels. Larger windows = smoother but spatially coarser results. Typical range: 32–256. Use a list like [32, 64, 128] for a batch sweep.
  4. Correlation feature: 1 = orientation image (recommended for DEMs — invariant to illumination); 0 = hillshade.
  5. Co-registration switch: 1 = enabled, 0 = disabled. Removes systematic offsets caused by GPS error or georeferencing inconsistency before DIC.
  6. Co-registration window: "bbox" uses the stable-ground region defined by coreg_bbox; "full" uses the entire image overlap.
  7. DFT upsampling factor for subpixel displacement precision. 4 = 0.25 px precision. Higher values increase accuracy but slow down processing.
  8. Controls output grid density: step = window_size / skip_factor. skip_factor: 4 with window_size: 64 gives a point every 16 px. Higher = denser grid.
  9. Master switch for post-processing. Set true to filter outlier vectors and produce GeoPackage / PNG outputs after DIC.

  base_run_tag: "MyProject_Optical"
  img_primary:  "/path/to/ortho_before.tif"
  img_secondary: "/path/to/ortho_after.tif"
  output_dir:   "/path/to/output"

batch:
  base_img_res: 10           # (1)!
  target_resolutions: [1]
  window_sizes: [32, 64]     # (2)!

dic_params:
  rescale_results: true
  OR: 0                      # (3)!
  co_f: 1
  co_os: 2
  coreg_method: "full"       # (4)!
  # coreg_bbox: [minx, miny, maxx, maxy]
  export_sparse_gpkg: true
  os: 4
  skip_factor: 4
  refcode: "EPSG:2056"       # (5)!
  auto_reproject_to_utm: false
  debug_mode: false
  n_workers: 1

  VectorFilter:
    Enabled: false           # (6)!
    OutputTxt: false
    OutputGpkg: true
    OutputPlot: false
    PlotResult: false
    HillshadeTif: "/path/to/ortho_before.tif"
    PlotWMS: false
    WMSLayer: "satellite"
    PlotHillshade: false
    PlotBackgroundXYZ: false
    BlackArrows: false       # (7)!
    MaxMagnitude: 50.0
    ColorMax: 5
    BackgroundAlpha: 0.8
    Downsample: 10
    ThrMin: -100
    ThrMax: 100
  1. Ground sampling distance of your input orthophotos in metres/pixel.
  2. Two window sizes in one batch run — 32 captures fine detail; 64 gives a smoother, more robust result. Compare the outputs to choose.
  3. Correlation feature: 0 = grayscale intensity (default for optical). Use 1 (orientation image) for textured scenes with strong illumination variation.
  4. Whole-image co-registration. Recommended for optical when the scene has a large stable area. Switch to "bbox" and uncomment coreg_bbox if only a small stable region is available.
  5. EPSG code of your input CRS. Change this to match your data — e.g. "EPSG:32632" for UTM zone 32N.
  6. Master switch for post-processing. Set true to filter outlier vectors and produce GeoPackage / PNG outputs after DIC.
  7. false = arrows coloured by magnitude. Often looks better on orthophotos than uniform black arrows.

    BackgroundAlpha: 0.6
    Downsample: 10
  1. Keep at 1.0 for non-georeferenced webcam images. All outputs are in pixels, not metres.
  2. How to handle frames of different sizes: "crop" to the common area (no black borders); "pad" extends the smaller frame with zeros.
  3. Co-registration is usually disabled for webcam imagery — camera position is fixed and frames are already aligned.
  4. Fixed value — do not change. Signals non-georeferenced pixel-coordinate mode throughout the pipeline.
  5. AI segmentation mask using a pretrained SegFormer model. When enabled, removes semantic regions (sky, water, snow) from DIC results.
  6. Semantic classes to exclude. Options: sky, water, snow, land, vegetation, buildings, mountain.
  7. Inference device: null = auto-detect (uses MPS on Apple Silicon, CUDA on NVIDIA GPU, falls back to CPU).
  8. Generates an animated GIF that blinks between the primary frame and the DIC overlay — useful for quick visual QC.
  9. Master switch for post-processing. Set true to filter outlier vectors and produce outputs after DIC.
  10. null = no magnitude cap. Set a value (e.g. 50.0) to hard-clip vectors above that pixel displacement.

docs.title: Running from a plugin installation
docs.text:
After installing the plugin via QGIS, the DIC scripts and Python environment are available without any separate setup.

The easiest way to get the correct invocation is the 📋 Copy Run Command button in the plugin dialog — it resolves the correct Python interpreter and script paths for your system automatically, regardless of QGIS version or installation location, and copies the full command to the clipboard.

docs.title: Script location

docs.title: Logging
docs.text: Each run writes a log file run_log_<timestamp>.txt in the output directory. The log includes all parameter values, per-window timing, and any warnings.

docs.title: Using the QGIS Plugin
docs.text:
This guide walks you through your first DIC run — from opening the plugin to loading displacement results in QGIS. Processing time depends on data size, resolution, and window settings.

Before starting, here is a quick overview of the main dialog components:

  • Plugin icon: Click the MOBI-DIC button in the QGIS toolbar to open the dialog.
  • Mode toggle: Switch between DEM, Optical, and Webcam processing modes.
  • Menu sidebar: Navigate between the three workflow stages: Processing, Visualisation, and Post-Processing.
  • Configuration panel: The main working area; expands into collapsible sections (Input/Output, DIC Parameters, Co-Registration, Vector Filter) depending on the active sidebar tab.
  • Run & Processing Log panel: Launch a run with ▶ Run DIC, load/save configurations, and monitor live log output. Access Settings and Help from the top-right buttons.

Input data requirements

  • DEM mode: Single-band GeoTIFFs, same CRS, spatially overlapping.
  • Optical mode: Single- or multi-band GeoTIFFs (converted to grayscale), same CRS, spatially overlapping.
  • Webcam mode: Any image format (JPEG, PNG, TIFF, …); no CRS needed; different sizes handled via align_mode.

See Input data requirements for full details.

docs.title: First run
docs.text:
1. Click the MOBI-DIC toolbar button to open the dialog.
  2. In the Input/Output tab, set the Primary input (pre-event DEM or image) and Secondary input (post-event). See Input/Output tab for time-series mode and all input options.

  3. Choose an Output directory and optionally edit the Run tag.

  4. In the DIC Parameters tab, review the resolution and window size settings. The plugin auto-detects the native resolution from the primary input. See DIC Parameters for co-registration and advanced options.

  5. Click ▶ Run DIC to start processing. Output appears in the log panel. The first run may take a little longer due to one-time initialisation.

  6. Once complete, switch to the Visualisation tab in the sidebar and open the Results Import sub-tab.

  7. Set the output directory and click Scan for Results to detect all displacement GeoTIFFs.

  8. Optionally filter by component, then click Load Selected into QGIS to add the layers with automatic symbology applied. See Results Import for symbology options and Google Earth export.

docs.title: Using the CLI
docs.text:
The CLI runs the same processing pipeline as the plugin, driven entirely by a YAML configuration file. It is suited for headless servers, automated workflows, or batch jobs sweeping multiple resolution and window size combinations.

The recommended way to get started is the 📋 Copy Run Command button at the bottom of the plugin dialog. It resolves the correct Python interpreter and script paths for your system automatically — regardless of QGIS version or installation location — writes the current settings to output_dir/last_run_config.yml, and copies the full shell command to the clipboard, ready to paste into a terminal or script.

Manual path lookup (advanced)

If you need to construct the command by hand, the plugin is installed inside the QGIS user profile directory and the bundled Python interpreter lives in ~/.slf-dic/. The profile path varies by platform and QGIS major version:

macOSLinuxWindows 
~/.slf-dic/.pixi/envs/default/bin/python3 \
  ~/Library/Application\ Support/QGIS/QGIS3/profiles/default/python/plugins/slfdic/_dic_scripts/run_dic4dem_processing.py \
  --config /path/to/config_dic4dem.yml

~/.slf-dic/.pixi/envs/default/bin/python3 \
  ~/.local/share/QGIS/QGIS3/profiles/default/python/plugins/slfdic/_dic_scripts/run_dic4dem_processing.py \
  --config /path/to/config_dic4dem.yml

%USERPROFILE%\.slf-dic\.pixi\envs\default\python.exe ^
  %APPDATA%\QGIS\QGIS3\profiles\default\python\plugins\slfdic\_dic_scripts\run_dic4dem_processing.py ^
  --config C:\path\to\config_dic4dem.yml

Tip

If you are running QGIS 4, replace QGIS3 in the path with QGIS4. If you are unsure where your profile directory is, open the QGIS Python console and run QgsApplication.qgisUserDatabaseFilePath() — the plugins folder is a sibling of that file.

Replace run_dic4dem_processing.py with run_dic4optical_processing.py or run_dic4webcam_processing.py for other modes.

See CLI & Batch Processing for a full walkthrough of batch runs and pipeline-only installations, and Configuration Reference for all available parameters.

docs.title: Expected outputs
docs.text:
Each run produces a directory under output_dir/ named after the run tag, containing:

* is a shorthand for {run_tag}_{date1}_{date2} throughout the table below.

File Description DIC_*.h5 Raw HDF5 results (sparse correlation grid) DIC_x_*.tif East–West (x) displacement (interpolated GeoTIFF) DIC_y_*.tif North–South (y) displacement DIC_xy_*.tif 2D horizontal displacement magnitude DIC_dz_*.tif Vertical displacement, raw (DEM mode only) DIC_z_*.tif Vertical displacement, co-registration restored (DEM mode only) DIC_xyz_*.tif 3D displacement magnitude (DEM mode only) DIC_az_*.tif Displacement azimuth (degrees from North) DIC_dip_*.tif Displacement dip angle (DEM mode only) DIC_ee_*.tif Correlation error (normalised RMS DFT error) DIC_sparse_*.gpkg Sparse displacement points (optional) DIC_coherence_filter_*.gpkg Coherence-filtered displacement vectors (optional) DIC_*_filtered.png Vector field plot (optional) *_log.txt Full processing log

For the physical meaning of each displacement component and how to interpret the EE quality layer, see Output components.

If something goes wrong, see the Troubleshooting guide.

docs.title: Pipeline Only Installation
docs.text:
This guide covers the headless installation of the MOBI-DIC processing pipeline without QGIS. Use this on servers or workstations where no graphical interface is available.

How to obtain a pipeline-only build

MOBI-DIC is currently not distributed publicly. A pipeline-only build is available on request, contact mobi-dic@slf.ch.

Access requires a signed Research EULA — see License & conditions for details.

docs.title: Step 1: Install pixi
docs.text:
pixi is the package manager used to create the Python environment. No admin rights are needed.

# macOS / Linux
curl -fsSL https://pixi.sh/install.sh | sh

# Windows (PowerShell)
iwr -useb https://pixi.sh/install.ps1 | iex

docs.title: Step 2: Unzip the distribution
docs.text:
unzip mobi-dic_v1.x.x_full_pipeline.zip
cd mobi-dic_v1.x.x_full_pipeline

docs.title: Step 3: Install the Python environment
docs.text:
pixi install

This creates a self-contained environment under .pixi/ in the current folder. All packages are pinned via the bundled pixi.lock — no manual dependency management needed.

docs.title: Step 4: Edit the configuration file
docs.text:
The config files are inside slf-dic-python/. Open the relevant one in a text editor and adjust the io section to point to your input files and output directory:

nano slf-dic-python/config_dic4dem.yml

See the Configuration Reference for a full description of all parameters.

docs.title: Step 5: Run the pipeline
docs.text:
cd slf-dic-python

# DEM-based DIC
pixi run python run_dic4dem_processing.py --config config_dic4dem.yml

# Optical image DIC
pixi run python run_dic4optical_processing.py --config config_dic4optical.yml

# Webcam / non-georeferenced image DIC (full build only)
pixi run python run_dic4webcam_processing.py --config config_dic4webcam.yml

Running with conda instead of pixi

If your server already has Conda/Mamba available and you prefer not to install pixi, you can create an environment manually: 

mamba create -n mobi-dic python=3.12 numpy scipy pandas geopandas rasterio \
  pyproj shapely gdal affine pillow scikit-image h5py pyyaml requests \
  tqdm joblib psutil matplotlib
conda activate mobi-dic
cd slf-dic-python
python run_dic4dem_processing.py --config config_dic4dem.yml

Licensed builds

Pipeline-only ZIPs with an embedded expiry date will stop running after the expiry date shown in VERSION.txt. Contact mobi-dic@slf.ch to request a renewal build.

docs.title: QGIS + CLI Installation
docs.text:
This guide covers the full MOBI-DIC installation including the QGIS plugin and the DIC Python processing environment. After completing these two steps you can run DIC directly from QGIS and from the command line.

How to obtain MOBI-DIC

MOBI-DIC is currently not distributed publicly. A QGIS + CLI build is available on request, contact mobi-dic@slf.ch.

Access requires a signed Research EULA — see License & conditions for details.

docs.title: Step 1: Install the plugin
docs.text:
1. Open QGIS
  2. Go to Plugins → Manage and Install Plugins
  3. Switch to the Install from ZIP tab
  4. Browse to the _plugin.zip file you received
  5. Click Install Plugin
  6. In the Installed tab, find MOBI-DIC and tick the checkbox to enable it.

A toolbar button (MOBI-DIC logo) will appear in the QGIS toolbar.

docs.title: Step 2: Install the DIC Python environment
docs.text:
The plugin needs a dedicated Python environment with the DIC processing libraries. This is downloaded automatically through the plugin — no terminal or administrator rights are required.

  1. Click the MOBI-DIC toolbar button to open the dialog

  2. Click the Settings button (⚙) in the top-right of the dialog

  3. In the Python Environment section, click Install DIC Environment

  4. Review the package summary and click Install. For a reference on what is installed on your machine, see Security.

  5. Wait for the installation to complete, this typically takes a few minutes. Progress is shown in the dialog.

After installation the status line shows ✓ Installed and ✓ Environment ready and the ▶ Run DIC button becomes available. Optionally click Test Python to verify the installation (it should report Python 3.12.13).

Environment location

The environment is stored in ~/.slf-dic/ (macOS/Linux) or %USERPROFILE%\.slf-dic\ (Windows) and survives plugin updates.

docs.title: Software Overview
docs.text:
MOBI-DIC is available in two builds. The Full (QGIS + CLI) build is the standard version for desktop users. The Pipeline Only build is for headless servers and automated workflows.

How to obtain MOBI-DIC

MOBI-DIC is currently not distributed publicly. The standard QGIS + CLI build is available on request — contact mobi-dic@slf.ch. If you need a pipeline-only build, please mention that in your request.

Access requires a signed Research EULA — see License & conditions for details.

Full (QGIS + CLI) — standard build

Includes the QGIS plugin, the interactive processing dialog, and the command-line pipeline. Recommended for most users.

→ QGIS + CLI Installation Guide

Pipeline Only — on request

Command-line only, no QGIS or graphical interface. For servers and automated batch workflows.

→ Pipeline Only Installation Guide

docs.title: System Requirements
docs.text:
Full (QGIS + CLI)

Component Requirement OS Windows 10/11 (x86_64) · macOS 12+ (Intel or Apple Silicon) · Linux (x86_64) QGIS 3.16 minimum; QGIS 4 recommended — download from qgis.org Internet Required once to download the DIC Python environment on first launch Disk ~1.4 GB for the Python environment

Pipeline Only

Component Requirement OS Linux x86_64 · macOS (Intel or Apple Silicon) · Windows x86_64 pixi Package manager used to create the Python environment — pixi.sh Internet Required once to download the Python environment Disk ~1.3 GB for the Python environment

Windows support

MOBI-DIC runs on all supported operating systems, but Windows is the least tested platform and may run slower due to differences in process handling and I/O performance. Linux or macOS is recommended for production workloads.

RAM

  • 8–16 GB: Small datasets (< 1 GB combined) with window sizes ≥ 32
  • 32–64 GB: Recommended for typical datasets (1–5 GB combined)
  • 128 GB+: Large datasets (> 10 GB combined) with small windows (8–16)

RAM usage scales with input data size and window size. Approximate peak RAM as a multiple of total input GeoTIFF size (primary + secondary combined):

Window size RAM multiplier 8 ×18.8 16 ×12.0 32 ×10.6 64–512 ×10–10.3

If RAM is limited, increase the window size or reduce the target resolution.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Common issues and how to resolve them.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
The ▶ Run DIC button stays greyed out after installing the environment

The button requires both inputs to be set and the Python environment to be marked as ready.

  1. Open Settings (⚙, top-right) and check the Python Environment section.
  2. The status line must show ✓ Installed and ✓ Environment ready.
  3. If it shows an error, click Install DIC Environment again or use Test Python to diagnose the issue.
  4. Also confirm that both Primary input and Secondary input are set in the Input/Output tab.
Installation fails or stalls
  • Check your internet connection — pixi downloads packages from conda-forge on first install.
  • If behind a corporate proxy, configure it in your system settings before installing.
  • Try deleting ~/.slf-dic/ (macOS/Linux) or %USERPROFILE%\.slf-dic\ (Windows) and reinstalling from scratch.

docs.title: Processing
docs.text:
All displacement values are near zero or exactly zero

The images likely did not correlate. Common causes:

  • Wrong mode — using DEM mode on optical images or vice versa.
  • No spatial overlap — primary and secondary extents do not intersect. Check in QGIS by loading both inputs.
  • Window too large — if window_size exceeds the overlapping area in pixels, all windows are masked.
  • Identical inputs — accidentally providing the same file as both primary and secondary.
Results show large striping or grid artefacts
  • The skip factor is too low relative to window size. Try skip_factor: 4 (default).
  • The oversampling (os) is too low for the displacement magnitude. Increase from 4 to 10.
  • In DEM mode, try switching OR from 0 (hillshade) to 1 (orientation) — orientation is less sensitive to illumination differences between acquisitions.
CRS mismatch warning in the log 

[CRS-MISMATCH] Primary DEM CRS (...) differs from secondary DEM CRS (...)
The two inputs are in different coordinate reference systems. MOBI-DIC processes them as-is, which will produce incorrect results. Reproject one file to match the other before running.

If your inputs are in a geographic CRS (degrees), enable auto_reproject_to_utm: true — the pipeline will reproject both files to UTM automatically.

Run crashes with a MemoryError or the machine becomes unresponsive

Peak RAM scales with input size and window size. Options to reduce memory:

  • Increase target_resolutions (e.g. [2] processes at half the native resolution, using ~4× less RAM).
  • Increase window_sizes — paradoxically, larger windows use less RAM per correlation call.
  • Reduce the spatial extent of inputs by cropping to the area of interest before processing.
  • See the RAM table in the installation guide for estimates.
The run is very slow
  • Each (resolution, window size) combination is a separate run. Reduce the batch sweep: use [1] for target_resolutions and a single value for window_sizes while tuning.
  • Increase n_workers to use multiple CPU threads (e.g. n_workers: 4). Start conservatively — high thread counts can increase memory pressure.
  • Increase skip_factor to reduce the number of correlation windows (e.g. 8 instead of 4).
  • Enable debug_mode: true to see per-step timing in the log and identify the bottleneck.
Co-registration produces an unreasonable shift

When coreg_method: full, the entire image overlap is used to estimate the bulk shift. If most of the overlap is moving (e.g. a landslide covering the whole scene), the estimated shift will be biased.

Switch to coreg_method: bbox and draw a bounding box over a clearly stable area (bedrock, buildings, road markings). This is the DEM-mode default for this reason.

docs.title: Outputs & Results
docs.text:
Output GeoTIFFs are empty or full of NoData
  • Check the log for any [WARNING] or [ERROR] lines — these usually identify the cause.
  • If the co-registration step reports a very large shift, the corrected secondary may fall outside the primary extent. Disable co-registration (co_f: 0) to check.
  • Confirm the two inputs actually overlap by loading them in QGIS.
Scan for Results finds no layers
  • Confirm the Output directory in the I/O tab points to the directory that contains the run sub-folders, not to the sub-folder itself.
  • The plugin scans recursively for DIC_*.tif — at least one completed run must exist.
  • If you moved or renamed the output folder after the run, update the Output directory field and scan again.

docs.title: Getting more help
docs.text:
If none of the above resolves your issue, open a GitHub Issue and include:

  • The full log from the run (saved to output_dir/run_log_<timestamp>.txt)
  • Your config YAML (the Save Config… button exports it)
  • QGIS version and operating system

docs.title: QGIS Plugin Overview
docs.text: The MOBI-DIC QGIS plugin provides a full graphical interface for the DIC processing pipeline. It is a QGIS plugin that runs the Python processor as a subprocess and communicates results back through the QGIS layer tree.

docs.title: Mode toggle
docs.text:
Select the processing pipeline that matches your input data type. The mode switch reconfigures the Input/Output and DIC Parameters groups so only the relevant fields are shown.

Mode Input type Outputs DEM Elevation model pairs (GeoTIFF) EW · NS · vertical displacement + 3-D magnitude Optical Orthoimage pairs (GeoTIFF) EW · NS displacement + 2-D magnitude Webcam Any image pairs (JPEG / PNG / TIFF) Pixel displacement (no CRS)

docs.title: Dialog layout
docs.text:
The dialog is organised into three sidebar sections accessed via the vertical navigation strip on the left. Each section groups related functionality, from configuring and launching a run, through inspecting results, to re-running post-processing steps.

Sidebar section Purpose Processing Configure inputs, algorithm parameters, co-registration, and the vector filter, then launch a run Visualisation Scan output GeoTIFFs, load them into QGIS with auto-symbology, and export to Google Earth Post-Processing Re-run the coherence filter or neighbour filter on existing results without reprocessing

docs.title: Processing
docs.text:
Set up a DIC run end-to-end: define inputs and outputs, tune the correlation algorithm, configure co-registration, and optionally apply a vector filter, then launch the batch processor from this panel.

Group Reference Input / Output Input files, output directory, run tag, single-pair or time-series mode DIC Parameters Resolution sweep, window sizes, correlation feature, oversampling Co-Registration Global shift correction settings and stable-ground bounding box Vector Filter Post-processing thresholds, GPKG / PNG export

docs.title: Visualisation
docs.text:
Load and present DIC outputs directly in QGIS. Results Import handles layer loading and Google Earth export; Map Layout Builder produces print-ready figures.

Sub-tab Purpose Results Import Scan output GeoTIFFs, load into QGIS with auto-symbology, and export to Google Earth Map Layout Builder Generate print-ready QGIS layouts with per-component panels, background map, scale bar, and north arrow

docs.title: Post-Processing
docs.text:
Apply or refine vector filtering on an existing DIC run without re-running the full correlation. Useful for adjusting filter thresholds after the fact or testing different settings on already-computed results.

Sub-tab Purpose Neighbourhood Coherence Filter (HDF5) Single-pass radius-based filter on the interpolated HDF5 grid Iterative Neighbour Filter (GPKG) Multi-pass N-nearest-neighbour filter on the sparse GeoPackage export

docs.title: Toolbar buttons
docs.text:
Quick-access actions at the bottom of the dialog for saving and loading configurations, launching runs, and opening help.

Button Action Load Config… Load a previously saved YAML config file (Ctrl+O) Save Config… Save all current dialog settings to a YAML file (Ctrl+S) 📋 Copy the equivalent shell command to the clipboard ▶ Run DIC Start processing (enabled when both inputs are set) ■ Cancel Interrupt the running subprocess ⚙ Settings Open the Settings dialog ? Help Open the About / Help panel — shows credits, a quick-start guide, a link to the online documentation, and support contact details

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
The Settings dialog (⚙) contains global preferences that apply across all runs and sessions. It is organised into five collapsible sections:

Section Purpose License Displays the installed license details — version, build date, enabled modes, and expiry date. Only visible when a license file is present. Python Environment Install or reinstall the DIC Python environment via pixi. Shows the current installation status, lets you set the script directory and Python executable manually, and provides a Test Python button to verify that all required packages are available. Processing Sets the number of parallel worker threads for the correlation loop (pixoff workers). Auto uses all available CPU cores. Also exposes a RAM-debug mode that logs memory usage per processing step — useful for diagnosing out-of-memory crashes on large inputs. Results Controls how layers are loaded after a run. Options include auto-loading results into QGIS on completion, the progress update interval, and the default colour range mode (Auto percentile or Fixed custom values) applied when scanning in the Results Import tab. Cache Shows the location and size of the plugin cache and provides an Empty Cache button to free disk space.

docs.title: Co-Registration
docs.text:
Co-registration removes the bulk offset between the primary and secondary image before the main DIC run. Without it, a systematic shift caused by GPS error, georeferencing inconsistency, or sensor drift is absorbed into all displacement estimates and biases every vector in the scene by the same amount. When enabled, the shift is estimated via DFT on a stable-ground region and applied to the secondary image before correlation begins.

The typical setup is:

  1. Enable co-registration (co_f = 1) — on by default for DEM and Optical mode.
  2. Choose a method — full if most of the scene is stable; bbox if a distinct stable-ground patch needs to be isolated.
  3. If using bbox, define the stable-ground bounding box by drawing on the canvas, loading a vector file, or entering coordinates manually.
  4. Optionally enable the error statistics plot to verify the co-registration converged correctly.

Default state

Co-registration is enabled by default for DEM and Optical mode and disabled for Webcam mode (non-georeferenced images have no georeferencing error to correct).

docs.title: Enable Co-Registration (co_f)
docs.text: Turns co-registration on or off. When disabled all other settings in this panel are ignored and the secondary image is used as-is.

docs.title: Oversampling (co_os)
docs.text:
Sub-pixel upsampling factor applied when estimating the bulk shift via DFT. Precision scales as \(\text{precision} = 1 / \texttt{co\_os}\) pixels — doubling the value halves the shift error. Higher values cost proportionally more computation.

Value Shift precision 1 1 pixel (integer only) 2 (default) 0.5 px 4 0.25 px 10 0.1 px

docs.title: Method
docs.text: Method Description When to use full Estimates the shift over the entire image overlap Most of the scene is stable; no obvious stable patch to isolate bbox (default for DEM) Estimates the shift only within a manually defined stable-ground bounding box Most of the scene is moving, using the full image would average moving and stable areas and underestimate the true offset

docs.title: Stable-Ground Bounding Box (coreg_bbox)
docs.text:
Active only when Method is set to bbox. Defines the region used to estimate the bulk shift. Coordinates are in the layer CRS (e.g. EPSG:2056 for Swiss LV95).

The box can be defined in three ways:

  • Draw on Canvas — digitise the box interactively on the QGIS map canvas
  • Browse GPKG / KML — load a GeoPackage or KML file; the bounding box of the entire layer is used as the stable-ground window
  • Manual entry — type the four coordinates directly
Field Meaning Min X / Max X West and east edges Min Y / Max Y South and north edges

Only the bounding box is used

Regardless of polygon shape or count, only the rectangular bounding box (min/max extent) of the layer is extracted — the actual geometry is ignored. A circular or irregular polygon gives the same result as a rectangle drawn around it. If the file contains multiple features, the bounding box spans all of them combined. To target a precise area, draw the box manually on the canvas instead.

How to choose a good stable-ground patch:

  • Select an area that is genuinely stable between the two acquisitions (bedrock outcrop, road, building roof).
  • The patch should be large enough to contain many DIC windows, at least a few hundred pixels on each side at the target resolution.
  • Avoid areas with shadows, water, snow, or vegetation change.
  • The patch does not need to be centred, a corner of the scene is fine as long as the surface is stable.

docs.title: Error Statistics Plot
docs.text:
When enabled, saves a PNG alongside the HDF5 output showing:

  • The stable-ground bounding box overlaid on the primary image
  • Histograms of the residual X, Y (and Z for DEM) displacement errors within the stable patch after co-registration

Use this plot to verify that the co-registration converged and that residual errors are centred near zero. Large residuals or a bimodal histogram indicate a poor stable-ground selection or an insufficient oversampling factor.

docs.title: DIC Parameters
docs.text:
The DIC Parameters tab controls the core correlation algorithm. Settings here determine the spatial resolution, the size of the correlation window, and the sub-pixel precision of the registration. They map directly to the batch and dic_params sections of the YAML config and are shared across all pairs in a batch run.

The typical setup is:

  1. Check the auto-detected base resolution — read from the primary input after it is set in the I/O tab.
  2. Set the target resolutions and window sizes to sweep (comma-separated lists for batch runs).
  3. Choose the correlation feature for DEM mode — hillshade or orientation image.
  4. Review oversampling and skip factor defaults; adjust only if sub-pixel accuracy or grid density requirements differ from the defaults.

docs.title: Correlation setup
docs.text:
Parameter Default Description Base resolution auto-detected Native ground sampling distance (GSD) of the input data. Auto-detected from the primary file geotransform when the input is set in the I/O tab. In Webcam mode fixed at 1 px/px and not editable. Target resolutions [1] Comma-separated list of output resolutions (m/px for DEM/Optical; px/px for Webcam). The input is resampled to each value before correlation. A value equal to the base resolution runs at native scale; a larger value downsamples first. Multiple values produce one scenario per entry. Window sizes (px) [64] Comma-separated list of correlation window side lengths in pixels. Larger windows are more robust against noise but give coarser spatial detail. Multiple values produce one scenario per entry. Correlation feature (OR) on / Orientation Controls which image representation is fed into DIC. Unchecked (OR=0) uses hillshade — an illumination image computed from the DEM (azimuth 315°, elevation 45°). Checked (OR=1) uses the orientation image — the sign of the spatial gradient — which is more robust when illumination changes between acquisitions (Dematteis et al., 2021).

Choosing window size and resolution

  • Window size should be at least 2–3× the expected maximum displacement in pixels at the chosen resolution. Too small → aliasing and noise; too large → loss of spatial detail.
  • Start with native resolution ([1]). Add a coarser resolution (e.g. [1, 2]) only if the run is slow or signal-to-noise is low at native scale.
  • For DEM data at 1 m resolution, WIN=64 covers a 64 m correlation patch and resolves displacements of a few centimetres to tens of metres.

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text: Parameter Default Description Export sparse GeoPackage on (DEM) Write the raw, pre-interpolation measurement points to a GeoPackage. Each point stores the displacement vector, sub-pixel quality metric, and geographic coordinates. Required as input for the Iterative Neighbour Filter. Sparse results only off Stop after the HDF5 and sparse GeoPackage are written. Gridfit interpolation, GeoTIFF outputs, and all post-processing filters are skipped. Automatically enables sparse GeoPackage export. Export velocity off Derive velocity rasters by dividing displacement by the date interval parsed from the file names. Velocity layers are written alongside each displacement component. Velocity unit m/year Normalisation unit for velocity rasters. m/year divides by elapsed years; m/day by elapsed days. In Webcam mode switches to px/year or px/day. Only visible when export velocity is enabled. Image alignment (Webcam only) crop How to handle a size mismatch between primary and secondary images. crop — both images are trimmed to the top-left common area. pad — the smaller image is zero-padded to match the larger.

docs.title: Algorithm settings
docs.text: Parameter Default Description DIC oversampling (os) 4 Sub-pixel upsampling factor inside the DFT registration step. Higher values achieve finer localisation at the cost of more computation. Values of 4–8 are typical. Skip factor 4 Controls the stride between successive windows: step = window_size / skip_factor pixels. Larger values produce sparser but faster results; smaller values produce denser, overlapping windows. Output CRS EPSG:2056 EPSG code for the output coordinate reference system. Auto-detected from the primary input. Change manually or via the Settings dialog if needed. Locked to pixel in Webcam mode. Auto-reproject to UTM on When the primary input uses a geographic CRS (degrees, e.g. WGS84 / EPSG:4326), automatically reproject to the nearest UTM zone so that pixel sizes are in metres. Has no effect on projected metric inputs.

docs.title: AI Segmentation Mask (Webcam mode only)
docs.text:
Uses a pretrained SegFormer model (ADE20K) to detect and exclude semantic regions from DIC results. Requires transformers and torch to be installed in the Python environment.

Experimental feature

The AI mask is experimental and results may vary depending on scene content, image quality, and lighting conditions. Snow detection in particular is unreliable — the model was not trained for snow-covered alpine terrain and frequently misclassifies shadowed snow, dirty snow, or rock/snow boundaries. Use the Save debug segmentation map option to inspect what the model detects before relying on the mask for production runs.

Parameter Default Description Enable AI segmentation mask off Activates semantic masking. Regions to exclude sky, water Semantic classes to mask out. Available: sky, water, snow, land, vegetation, buildings, mountain. Snow brightness min (V) 200 Minimum HSV brightness (0–255) for colour-based snow detection. Lower to also catch shadowed or dirty snow. Only active when snow is selected. Snow saturation max (S) 40 Maximum HSV saturation (0–255) for colour-based snow detection. Raise to catch bluish or yellowish snow patches. Only active when snow is selected. Device auto Torch inference device. auto uses CUDA if available, then MPS, then CPU. Mask dilation (px) 0 Expand each detected mask region by N pixels. Useful when mask edges are under-detected (e.g. at a water boundary). 0 = disabled. Save debug segmentation map off Saves a false-colour PNG of the full segmentation map and logs the top-15 detected ADE20K classes. Use this to diagnose which classes to add or remove.

docs.title: Input / Output
docs.text:
The Input / Output tab is where every processing run starts. It defines the input images or DEMs, the output directory, and whether to process a single image pair or a full time series. Once configured here, the run can be launched from the toolbar.

The typical setup is:

  1. Select a processing mode (DEM, Optical, or Webcam) using the mode toggle at the top of the dialog.
  2. Browse for the primary (pre-event) and secondary (post-event) input files, or populate the time-series table with multiple pairs.
  3. Set the output directory and optionally a run tag.
  4. Click ▶ Run DIC in the toolbar to start processing.

docs.title: Input data requirements
docs.text:
Requirements differ by processing mode:

DEMOpticalWebcam Requirement Detail Format GeoTIFF (.tif / .tiff) Bands Single-band (elevation values) CRS Both files must share the same CRS. A mismatch is logged as a warning and processing continues, but results will be incorrect. Geographic CRS Inputs in degrees (e.g. WGS84) are automatically reprojected to the appropriate UTM zone when auto_reproject_to_utm is enabled. Spatial overlap Primary and secondary must overlap. Only the overlapping extent is processed. No-data Cells with the raster nodata value or value 0 are treated as NaN and excluded from correlation. Requirement Detail Format GeoTIFF (.tif / .tiff) Bands Single-band (grayscale) or multi-band (e.g. RGB). Multi-band images are converted to grayscale via standard luminance weighting (0.299 R + 0.587 G + 0.114 B). Only the first three bands are used, band 4 and above (e.g. NIR, alpha) are ignored. CRS Both files must share the same CRS. Geographic CRS Same automatic UTM reprojection as DEM mode. Spatial overlap Primary and secondary must overlap. No-data Cells with the raster nodata value or value 0 are treated as NaN and excluded. Requirement Detail Format Any PIL-readable image: JPEG, PNG, TIFF, BMP, etc. No GeoTIFF or CRS required. Bands Any number; images are converted to RGB then grayscale internally. CRS None — all outputs are in pixel coordinates. Image size Primary and secondary may differ in size. Use align_mode: crop (default) to clip both to the top-left common area, or align_mode: pad to zero-pad the smaller image.

docs.title: Single-pair mode
docs.text: Field Description Primary input Pre-event DEM or image (GeoTIFF). Sets the reference CRS and pixel size. Secondary input Post-event DEM or image (GeoTIFF). Must overlap spatially with the primary. Output directory Directory where result sub-folders are written. Run tag Short label prepended to output file names. Auto-generated from parameters if left blank.

docs.title: Time-series mode
docs.text:
Switch to Time Series mode to process multiple pairs in sequence. A table lists the pairs, each with an automatically generated tag derived from file names (date detection: YYYYMMDD or YYYY-MM-DD patterns).

Use the + / − buttons to add or remove pairs. The order in the table determines the processing sequence.

docs.title: Output naming
docs.text:
Run tags are auto-generated following this pattern:

{base_tag}_RES{res}_WIN{wi}_SKF{skip}_OR{or}_COF{co_f}[_COREG{method}]

For example: MyRun_RES1.0_WIN64_SKF1_OR0_COF1_COREGfull

docs.title: Map Layout Builder
docs.text:
The Map Layout Builder generates print-ready QGIS map layouts directly from DIC results. It arranges displacement components into a panel grid, adds a shared colorbar, scale bar, north arrow, and an optional background map, and opens the result in the QGIS Print Layout window where it can be exported to PDF or PNG.

The workflow is straightforward:

  1. Set the Directory and click Scan for Results to discover available timesteps and components.
  2. Choose a Layout mode to control how components and timesteps are arranged across pages.
  3. Configure page size, background map, colour ranges, and map extent.
  4. Click Build Layout — the layout opens in QGIS and is ready to export.

The tab is organised into four collapsible sections covering these steps in order.

docs.title: 1 · Select Data
docs.text: Define which DIC results to include in the layout and how they should be arranged. Scan the output directory first — this populates the timestep and component lists that all other sections depend on.

docs.title: Data type
docs.text: Option Description Displacement results Cumulative displacement layers (DIC_x, DIC_y, etc.) in metres Velocity results Layers produced by the Velocity Calculator; units shown as m/yr or m/day

docs.title: Directory & scan
docs.text: Point Directory to the root folder of a DIC processing run, then click Scan for Results. The scan searches recursively for all DIC_*.tif files underneath it and populates the timestep and component dropdowns. The title and subtitle fields are auto-filled from the run tag at this point.

docs.title: Layout mode
docs.text:
Controls how the scanned DIC layers are arranged across pages:

Mode Description All components for one timestep All displacement components in an auto-fitted grid on a single page. Select which timestep to show from the dropdown. All timesteps, all components One page per timestep, each with the full component grid. Available when multiple timesteps are found. One component across all timesteps One panel per timestep, all showing the same component. Select the component from the dropdown. Custom selection Manually tick the exact files to include, filtered by component. Grid dimensions can be overridden in Page Setup.

docs.title: 2 · Page Setup
docs.text:
Set the paper format, orientation, panel grid dimensions, and the title and subtitle text that appear at the top of the layout. For most cases the Auto grid setting produces a well-balanced arrangement without manual adjustment.

Setting Description Page size Standard paper format (A4, A3, Letter, …) or Custom with manual width × height in mm Orientation Portrait or Landscape Grid Cols × Rows for the panel grid — set both to Auto (0) to let the builder choose the best fit Title Large bold text at the top of the first page; auto-filled from the run tag after scanning Subtitle Smaller text below the title, typically showing DIC run parameters; auto-filled from the run tag

docs.title: 3 · Map Settings
docs.text:
Control what is shown behind and around the displacement data — background map, spatial extent, coordinate grid, scale bar, north arrow, and layer transparency. The extent is computed automatically from the selected layers by default.

Setting Description Background Base map rendered behind DIC results: swisstopo, SwissImage, SwissAlti3D hillshade, OpenStreetMap, None, or a custom local raster. Swiss options require EPSG:2056 and an internet connection. Extent Auto — bounding box of selected layers (recommended); Canvas — current QGIS map view; File — bounding box of the first feature in a GPKG / SHP / KML file Buffer Extra margin added to each side of the computed extent in metres Map grid Optional coordinate grid overlay; set interval to 0 for Auto Cartographic Toggle scale bar and north arrow independently; both are hidden automatically in Webcam / pixel-coordinate mode Layer opacity Transparency of the DIC raster overlay (default 80 %)

docs.title: 4 · Colours & Ranges
docs.text:
Override the colormap and colour range for each displacement component independently. Use this to ensure consistent symbology across layouts regardless of the data range in individual files.

Overrides the colormap and Min/Max range for each component independently. Settings here apply only to the generated layout and do not affect the symbology of layers already loaded in QGIS.

Defaults match the component-specific colormaps from the Results Import tab.

docs.title: Building the layout
docs.text: Click Build Layout at the bottom of the tab. The builder creates a new QGIS Print Layout named after the run tag and opens it. From there use Layout → Export as PDF or Export as Image to save the output.

docs.title: Post-Processing
docs.text:
Re-run vector filtering on existing DIC results without repeating the full correlation. Both filters work independently from the Processing pipeline — you point them at output files from a previous run, tune the thresholds, and produce a new filtered GeoPackage that can be loaded directly into QGIS or exported to Google Earth.

Two sub-tabs are available, each targeting a different output format:

Sub-tab Input Algorithm Neighbourhood Coherence Filter HDF5 grid Single-pass radius-based coherence filter Iterative Neighbour Filter Sparse GeoPackage Multi-pass N-nearest-neighbour similarity filter

docs.title: Neighbourhood Coherence Filter (HDF5)
docs.text:
Operates on the interpolated displacement grid stored in HDF5 files. For each vector, all neighbours within a search radius of skip_factor × RadiusMult are found. The vector is rejected if it deviates from the local neighbourhood mean beyond the set direction or amplitude threshold. A global amplitude range and a hard magnitude cap are applied on top. The filter runs in a single pass.

Relation to the Vector Filter tab

This is the same algorithm available in the Processing → Vector Filter tab. Post-Processing mode lets you re-run it with different parameters on already-computed HDF5 files without redoing the DIC correlation.

docs.title: 1 · Input HDF5 Files
docs.text:
Select the HDF5 result files to filter. Files can be added individually or by scanning an entire folder.

Add one or more HDF5 result files produced by a previous DIC run.

Button Action Add File(s)… Browse and select individual .h5 / .hdf5 files Add from Folder… Recursively scan a folder and add all HDF5 files found Remove Selected Remove highlighted entries from the list

Current limitation

The filter currently processes only the first file in the list. Support for batch processing of multiple files is planned for a future release.

docs.title: 2 · Filter Parameters
docs.text:
Tune the amplitude, direction, and neighbourhood thresholds that control which vectors are rejected.

Parameter Default Description ThrMin (m) −100 m Lower amplitude bound. Vectors with magnitude below this value are excluded from all outputs. ThrMax (m) 100 m Upper amplitude bound. Vectors with magnitude above this value are excluded from all outputs. MaxMagnitude (m) 10 m Hard cap applied before neighbourhood comparison. Vectors exceeding this magnitude are removed entirely. ColorMax (m) 10 m Upper limit of the plot colourbar. Does not affect which vectors are exported. DirThr (°) 180° Direction coherence threshold. Vectors deviating more than this angle from the neighbourhood circular mean direction are rejected. Set to 180° to disable direction filtering. AmpThr (m) 5 m Amplitude coherence threshold. Vectors deviating more than this value from the neighbourhood mean amplitude are rejected. RadiusMult 5 Controls the search radius: radius = skip_factor × RadiusMult. Larger values include more distant neighbours. Downsample 1 Keep every N-th vector in all outputs. Does not affect filtering, only output density.

docs.title: 3 · Export Options
docs.text:
Choose which output files are written and how displacement arrows are styled when loading into QGIS or exporting to Google Earth.

Option Description Export GeoPackage (.gpkg) Write filtered vectors as a georeferenced vector layer. Required for QGIS loading and Google Earth export. Enabled by default. Export text (.txt) Write filtered vectors as a plain-text table. Save plot (.png) Render the filtered displacement field overlaid on a hillshade and save as PNG. Arrow style Black arrows — uniform black, good for simple overviews. Colored by field — arrows graduated by 2-D or 3-D magnitude.

Output files are written to the same folder as the input HDF5, named DIC_coherence_filter{run_tag}.gpkg.

Large vector counts and Google Earth performance

Google Earth Pro can become slow or unresponsive with more than a few thousand arrows. Use the Downsample parameter to thin the output before exporting — a value of 2–5 typically keeps the KMZ responsive while still conveying the displacement pattern.

docs.title: Running and loading results
docs.text:
Click ▶ Run Filter to start. Progress is streamed to the log panel. Once the run completes successfully:

  • ▶ Load in QGIS — loads the output GeoPackage as a vector arrow layer into the QGIS layer tree, coloured by the selected field.
  • 🌍 Export to Google Earth… — saves the output as a KMZ with scaled displacement arrows. You will be prompted for an arrow scale factor (1 = true map-unit length; increase to make short displacements visible).

docs.title: Iterative Neighbour Filter (GPKG)
docs.text:
Operates on the sparse point layer exported as a GeoPackage. For each displacement vector, the N nearest neighbours within a maximum search distance are evaluated. Vectors deviating from the neighbourhood mean beyond the set magnitude or direction threshold are rejected. Points with fewer than the minimum number of neighbours within the search distance are always removed. The algorithm processes highest-magnitude vectors first and can run for multiple iterations, each pass refining using only the survivors of the previous one.

Relation to the Vector Filter tab

This is the same algorithm available in the Processing → Vector Filter tab (algorithm by Nicolas Oestreicher). Post-Processing mode lets you re-run it on an existing GeoPackage without re-running DIC.

docs.title: 1 · Input
docs.text:
Browse to the sparse GeoPackage to filter and select which magnitude field to use for neighbourhood comparison.

Field Description GPKG file Browse to the sparse GeoPackage produced by the DIC export step. The file must contain az and xy (and optionally xyz) fields. Magnitude field Column used for neighbourhood magnitude comparison. xy = 2-D horizontal magnitude (√(dx²+dy²)); xyz = 3-D magnitude using the restored Z component — DEM mode only.

docs.title: 2 · Filter Parameters
docs.text:
Set the magnitude and direction thresholds, neighbourhood search distance, and number of filter passes.

Parameter Default Description Magnitude threshold 10 m Maximum allowed magnitude deviation from the neighbourhood mean. Direction threshold 15° Maximum allowed azimuth deviation from the neighbourhood circular mean. Min neighbours 4 Vectors with fewer neighbours within Max distance are removed regardless of magnitude or direction. Max distance 50 m Search radius for finding neighbours. Should match the point spacing of the sparse layer (skip_factor × resolution). Iterations 1 Number of filter passes. Each pass refines using only the survivors of the previous one. More passes remove more outliers but can over-thin dense displacement fields. Real-time deletion off When enabled, rejected points are removed from the search index immediately during a pass. When disabled, all decisions within a pass use the same snapshot. Real-time mode is order-dependent and slower.

docs.title: 3 · Export Options
docs.text:
Control how displacement arrows are styled when loading the filtered result into QGIS or exporting to Google Earth.

Option Description Arrow style Black arrows — uniform black. Colored by field — arrows graduated by the selected magnitude field. Color by field xy (2-D magnitude) or xyz (3-D magnitude, DEM mode only). Controls arrow colour when loading in QGIS or exporting to Google Earth.

Output is written to the same folder as the input GeoPackage, named {input_name}_neighbour.gpkg.

Large vector counts and Google Earth performance

Google Earth Pro can become slow or unresponsive with dense displacement fields. If the input GeoPackage is large, increase Min neighbours or reduce Max distance to produce a sparser result, or run an additional pass (more iterations) to remove more outliers before exporting.

docs.title: Running and loading results
docs.text:
Click ▶ Run Filter to start. Progress is streamed to the log panel. Once complete:

  • ▶ Load in QGIS — loads the output GeoPackage as a vector arrow layer, coloured by the selected field.
  • 🌍 Export to Google Earth… — saves the output as a KMZ. You will be prompted for an arrow scale factor.

docs.title: Results Import
docs.text:
The Results Import tab is the starting point for inspecting DIC outputs inside QGIS. After a processing run has completed, point it to the output directory and scan for results. You can then select individual displacement components, configure their colour scale and range, and load them directly into the QGIS layer tree with one click. From the same tab you can also export layers to Google Earth Pro as georeferenced KMZ overlays, optionally with time slider support for multi-date datasets.

The workflow is straightforward:

  1. Set the Directory and click Scan for Results to discover all available layers.
  2. Tick the components you need and click ▶ Load Selected into QGIS.
  3. Optionally click 🌍 Export to Google Earth Pro… to create KMZ files from the scanned layers.

The tab is organised into three collapsible sections covering these steps in order.

docs.title: 1 · Scan & Select Layers
docs.text: Discover and select the displacement layers to load. Point the plugin to the output directory, trigger a scan, and choose which components to bring into QGIS.

docs.title: Directory & scan
docs.text: Point Directory to the root folder of a DIC processing run and click Scan for Results. The scan searches recursively for all DIC_*.tif files and populates the layer list. Range computation for the Symbology table is also triggered at this point.

docs.title: Component filter
docs.text: Narrows the layer list to a specific displacement component or result type. After scanning, only components actually found in the directory are offered as options.

docs.title: Layer list
docs.text: Tick the layers you want to load, then click ▶ Load Selected into QGIS. Use the All / None / Invert buttons to manage the selection quickly. Layers are loaded into a named group in the QGIS layer tree.

docs.title: Output components
docs.text:
Each DIC run produces one GeoTIFF per displacement component:

Layer Modes Physical meaning DIC_x DEM, Optical East–West displacement. Positive = eastward. DIC_y DEM, Optical North–South displacement. Positive = northward. DIC_xy DEM, Optical 2-D horizontal magnitude: \(\sqrt{x^2 + y^2}\). Always ≥ 0. DIC_dz DEM only Vertical displacement before co-registration offset is restored. DIC_z DEM only Vertical displacement after co-registration offset is restored — the physically meaningful value. DIC_xyz DEM only 3-D magnitude: \(\sqrt{x^2 + y^2 + z^2}\). Always ≥ 0. DIC_az DEM, Optical Displacement azimuth in degrees clockwise from North (0–360°). DIC_dip DEM only Displacement dip angle from horizontal (−90° to +90°). Positive = upward. DIC_ee DEM, Optical Correlation error — normalised RMS residual from the DFT registration.

EE (correlation error): What it measures

EE is the normalised RMS registration error from the DFT cross-correlation algorithm (Guizar-Sicairos et al. 2008):

\[\mathrm{EE} = \sqrt{\left|1 - \frac{|\mathrm{CC}_\max|^2}{E_\text{ref} \cdot E_\text{sec}}\right|}\]

where \(\mathrm{CC}_\max\) is the cross-correlation peak value and \(E_\text{ref}\), \(E_\text{sec}\) are the total spectral energies of the reference and secondary image windows. A value of 0 means a perfect correlation peak; 1 means no correlation at all.

EE always reflects the quality of the 2-D image correlation — for Optical and Webcam mode this is the orthoimage patch; for DEM mode it is the hillshade or orientation image used as the correlation feature. It is therefore an XY-plane quality indicator in all modes and does not directly reflect the vertical displacement quality in DEM results.

A more representative quality metric is planned for a future release.

docs.title: 2 · Symbology & Display
docs.text: Configure the colormap and colour range applied to each component before loading. Each component has sensible defaults but can be overridden per-component or globally with a custom QML file.

docs.title: Symbology table
docs.text:
Each component row has four configurable columns:

Column Description Colormap Named colour scale or a custom QML file Min / Max Values mapped to the two ends of the colour ramp Range Auto — computed from raster data at load time; Fixed — uses the entered Min/Max

Default colormaps per component:

Component Default colormap Notes X, Y, Z, dZ RdBu (diverging) Range centred at zero XY, XYZ Deformation QML Magnitude — always ≥ 0 AZ AZ bundled QML Fixed 0–360° DIP DIP bundled QML Fixed −90° to +90° EE YlOrRd Fixed 0–1

In Auto mode, symmetric components (X, Y, Z, dZ) are automatically centred at zero: bound = max(|p5|, |p95|), range set to [−bound, +bound]. AZ, DIP, and EE always keep their fixed defaults regardless of this setting.

Use ↺ Reset ranges to Auto to clear any manually entered values and recompute from data.

docs.title: Layer opacity
docs.text: Transparency applied to every raster layer when loaded (default 80 %). Lower values let the basemap show through.

docs.title: Custom QML override
docs.text: Enable Override with custom QML for all layers and browse to a .qml file to apply a single style to every loaded layer, bypassing the per-component table.

docs.title: Global settings
docs.text:
The Settings → Results section sets defaults applied on every scan:

Setting Default Description Default range mode Auto Fixed or Auto for all components Percentile range 5 % – 95 % Low/high percentile bounds used in Auto mode Custom default ranges (table) Per-component Min/Max used in Fixed mode; Reset restores built-in defaults

Range computation uses GDAL's histogram method — no full raster read is needed; overviews are used where available.

docs.title: 3 · Google Earth Export
docs.text:
Export selected layers as georeferenced KMZ overlays for Google Earth Pro. Supports time slider animation for multi-date datasets and an embedded colormap legend.

Select one or more layers in the list and click 🌍 Export to Google Earth Pro… to create a georeferenced KMZ overlay and load it automatically in Google Earth Pro for a quick 3D visualisation with a legend indication.

Option Description TimeSpan tags Adds KML <TimeSpan> tags so Google Earth Pro can animate layers using its time slider. Dates are extracted automatically from output subdirectory names (format YYYYMMDD). Requires at least two dates in the directory name. Embed colormap legend Inserts the colour bar as a screen overlay inside each KMZ, positioned in the bottom-left corner with component name, unit, and min/max values.

Tip

For a full time series, export all layers at once — each component gets its own KMZ plus a master KML that links them. Use the master KML in Google Earth to keep file sizes small and toggle layers independently.

docs.title: Vector Filter
docs.text:
The Vector Filter removes outlier displacement vectors after DIC and produces cleaned vector outputs as GeoPackage, text, and PNG. It runs as an optional last step within the Processing pipeline, directly after the correlation. Two filter algorithms are available; the choice depends on whether you want to work on the interpolated grid or the sparse point layer.

The typical setup is:

  1. Select a filter mode from the dropdown — Neighbourhood Coherence Filter for grid-based filtering, Iterative Neighbour Filter for sparse-point filtering.
  2. Tune the filter parameters — thresholds for magnitude, direction, and neighbourhood radius or distance.
  3. Choose which output files to produce — GeoPackage, text, and/or PNG plot.
  4. The filter runs automatically at the end of each DIC processing run.

Note

The Vector Filter can also be re-run on existing results without reprocessing — use the Post-Processing sidebar.

docs.title: Filter mode
docs.text: Option Description Disabled No filtering — all vectors are passed through as-is Neighbourhood Coherence Filter Single-pass, radius-based filter operating on the interpolated HDF5 grid. Each vector is compared to neighbours within skip_factor × RadiusMult; vectors deviating too much in direction or amplitude from the local mean are rejected. Iterative Neighbour Filter Multi-pass N-nearest-neighbour similarity filter operating on the sparse GeoPackage export (export_sparse_gpkg is auto-enabled). Progressively refines the result over multiple passes. Algorithm by Nicolas Oestreicher.

docs.title: Neighbourhood Coherence Filter
docs.text:
Single-pass filter working on the interpolated grid (HDF5 output). For each vector, all neighbours within the search radius are found; vectors deviating from the local mean in direction or amplitude are rejected.

Parameter Description Max magnitude Hard cap applied first, before any neighbourhood comparison. Vectors exceeding this displacement magnitude (m) are removed entirely. Threshold min Lower amplitude bound. Vectors with magnitude below this value are excluded from all outputs. Threshold max Upper amplitude bound. Vectors with magnitude above this value are excluded from all outputs. Direction threshold Each vector is compared to the circular mean direction of its neighbours. Vectors deviating by more than this angle (°) are rejected. Set to 180° to disable direction filtering. Amplitude threshold Vectors whose magnitude differs from the local neighbourhood mean by more than this value (m) are rejected. Works together with the direction threshold. Radius multiplier Controls the neighbourhood search radius: radius = skip_factor × multiplier. Larger values include more distant neighbours. Arrow downsample (N) Keep every N-th vector in all outputs (GPKG, TXT, and plot). Does not affect filtering, only output density.

docs.title: Iterative Neighbour Filter
docs.text:
Multi-pass filter working on the sparse GeoPackage export. For each vector, the N nearest neighbours within the max distance are evaluated; vectors deviating too much in magnitude or azimuth are rejected. The process repeats for the configured number of iterations.

Note

Enabling this filter automatically turns on export_sparse_gpkg — the sparse GeoPackage is required as input.

Parameter Default Description Magnitude field xy Column from the sparse GeoPackage used for neighbourhood comparison. xy = 2-D horizontal magnitude (√(dx²+dy²)); xyz = 3-D magnitude using the co-registration-restored Z component — DEM mode only. Magnitude threshold 10 m Maximum allowed magnitude deviation from the neighbourhood mean. Direction threshold 15° Maximum allowed azimuth deviation from the neighbourhood circular mean. Min neighbours 4 Vectors with fewer than this many neighbours within Max distance are removed. Max distance 50 m Search radius for finding neighbours (map units / pixels). Iterations 1 Number of filter passes. More passes remove more outliers but can over-thin dense displacement fields.

docs.title: Export files
docs.text: Option Description Save as .txt Write filtered vectors as tab-separated text (x, y, dx, dy, magnitude columns). Save as GeoPackage Write filtered vectors as a GeoPackage vector layer with full CRS. Save result plot as .png Render the filtered displacement field overlaid on a background image and save as PNG.

docs.title: Plot settings
docs.text: Parameter Description Colour scale max Upper limit of the plot colourbar. Vectors above this value are clipped to the top colour; does not affect which vectors are exported. Black arrows When checked, all arrows are drawn in black. When unchecked, arrows are colour-coded by magnitude. Black arrows are useful when the background raster already carries colour information. Background alpha Opacity of the displacement magnitude colour overlay behind the arrows (0 = transparent, 1 = opaque). Plot hillshade from DSM Compute a shaded-relief image from the raster below and blend it into the background. Background DSM/raster Path to a GeoTIFF used as the hillshade source — typically the primary DEM or orthoimage. Overlay 3D displacement magnitude Colour-code the background by 3-D displacement magnitude (DEM mode only). Fetch WMTS/WMS background tile Download a web map tile as the plot background (requires internet). WMTS/WMS layer Tile style: satellite (aerial imagery), map (OpenStreetMap-style), or relief (terrain shading).
